summary: This unit teaches you to keep housekeeping supplies in the right place, in the right amount and in good condition. You will learn the types of supplies, how to set and use par, minimum and maximum levels, how to stock trolleys and floor pantries, how to requisition, receive, count and record stock, how to store and dilute chemicals safely, and how to control cost, waste and loss.

blocks.p: A room cannot be cleaned without cloths, chemicals, linen and guest supplies. If something runs out, the attendant walks to the store, the room is late, and the guest waits. If too much is bought, money is tied up and items go out of date or are spoiled. **Maintaining supplies** means having the right items, in the right amount, in the right place, at the right time, safe and in good condition.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees working as room attendants, villa attendants or housekeeping assistants. You may work in a large hotel with a main store and a floor pantry on every floor, or in a small villa where one cupboard holds everything. The ideas are the same.

Examples
How they are stored and used

Toilet rolls, facial tissue, paper towels
Bin liners, laundry bags, sanitary bags
Kept off the floor in a dry place, because damp and pests spoil them.
Floor cleaner, glass cleaner, bowl cleaner
Kept in labelled containers, low down, closed, apart from linen, amenities and food. A locked store for concentrates.

ul: **Consumables** are used up or given away: soap, toilet rolls, chemicals, bin liners, coffee sachets.
**Non-consumables (durables)** are used again and again: linen, mops, vacuum cleaners, irons. They wear out or get lost, so they are counted and checked, not just used up.

blocks.p: A hotel sets a **room standard list** (what each room gets, for each type of room and each day) and a **trolley standard list** (what each trolley carries). Standard lists mean every room is supplied the same way, every guest gets the same standard, and an attendant has what she needs without extra trips. Follow them. If a guest asks for more, give it and record what you gave, as the property's rules say.

blocks.note: Never put supplies for guests in the same cupboard as dirty linen, chemicals or rubbish. Germs and smells pass to clean items and chemicals can spoil or contaminate them.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Stock levels and the maths of supplies

blocks.p: Housekeeping uses four stock figures. Learn what each one means and how to work it out.

head: Level
What it means
Example
rows: The set amount that should always be kept in a pantry or on a trolley. Each day you restock back up to par.
Floor pantry par for toilet rolls: 100
The lowest amount to hold. Below this you risk running out.
The most you should hold, so space and money are not wasted.
The amount at which a new order or requisition is made, so stock arrives before you run out.

blocks.note: Par is used for floor pantries and trolleys that are topped up every day. Minimum, maximum and reorder levels are used mostly in the main store, where orders take time to arrive. Your property's words may differ: ask your supervisor.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Par for a pantry = daily use x the days between restocks, plus a small safety amount if the supervisor allows.

head: Step
Example
rows: 22 rooms occupied x 3 toilet rolls per room = 66 rolls a day
2. Multiply by the days between restocks
3. Add a safety amount if set

blocks.p: **Requisition = par - stock on hand.** If par is 90 bars of soap and the count at the end of the day is 38, requisition 90 - 38 = **52** bars.

head: Question
How to work it out
Example
rows: How many of one item for one day?
Occupied rooms x amount per room
Add up the daily occupied rooms, then multiply by the amount per room
Rooms for the week 121 x 2 toilet rolls = 242
How many bottles can be filled?
Large container in ml / bottle size in ml

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, and write the unit (rolls, bars, bottles, litres) with each answer. Check that the answer makes sense: if one room needs 3 rolls, 20 rooms cannot need 6.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **stock card** records every movement of one item: what came in, what went out and the balance.
New balance = old balance + received - issued. The balance on the card should match the count on the shelf. If it does not, find out why.

Housekeeping uses the front office **occupancy forecast** (the number of rooms expected to be occupied each day) to plan. More guests means more supplies used. Extra supplies are planned for busy times and events: the winter tourist season, holidays such as Easter and Christmas, weddings and conferences, and big events such as Reggae Sumfest in Montego Bay or other festivals. Quiet periods, such as after the season or in low months, need less stock.

blocks.note: A hurricane warning is a planning event too. Properties check that water, torches, batteries, cleaning supplies and spare linen are on hand, and follow their hurricane plan.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The trolley is the attendant's mobile store. It is stocked to the **standard list** before the shift and checked during it, so she can clean each room without going back and forth.

head: Part of the trolley
What goes there
rows: Guest amenities and room supplies in a tray or caddy
Clean, folded items for the rooms
Clean linen: sheets, pillowcases, towels, bath mats
Heavy items: bottles, buckets, vacuum cleaner, refills
Labelled spray bottles and cloths, kept closed and out of reach of guests
Soiled linen bag and waste bag, kept apart from clean items

flow: Wash and dry your hands
Check the standard list
Wipe the trolley clean
Load heavy items low
Load clean linen and amenities
Fill and label the spray bottles
Check the vacuum and equipment work
Lock or park the trolley safely

ul: Park the trolley **against the wall by the open door** of the room you are cleaning, so it does not block the corridor or fire exits and you can watch it.
Never leave the trolley unattended and unlocked with chemicals showing.
Keep clean and soiled linen apart.
Check stock during the shift and top up at the pantry if low.
At the end of the shift, put the trolley away, empty it, restock for the next shift, and return the key.

blocks.p: The **floor pantry** is a small room or cupboard on each guest floor. It holds the day's linen, amenities, paper goods and equipment so that attendants do not have to go to the main store for each room.

ul: Keep it **locked** when nobody is inside, and record every issue.
Keep shelves labelled, clean and tidy. Leave gaps so you can clean and look for pests.
Keep chemicals low down, apart from linen and amenities, in labelled containers.
Keep linen and paper off the floor.
Count it at set times and fill it back to par.

blocks.p: A **requisition** is a written request for stock, signed by an authorised person. The store issues stock **only against a signed requisition**, so every item is approved and recorded.

head: Form
What it shows
rows: What is needed, how many, for which pantry, who asked, date
What was given out, how many, to whom, when, and who signed
Movements and the balance for one item
What the store orders from a supplier
What the supplier says was delivered
What the supplier asks the hotel to pay

flow: Count the pantry and work out the shortage
Write the requisition and sign it
Supervisor approves
Store issues the stock and the storekeeper signs the issue sheet
Check items and quantities as they are handed over
Sign for the stock and put it in the pantry
Update the records

blocks.p: When supplies come from a supplier, someone checks them before they are put away. In a small property, that may be you.

flow: Check the delivery note against the purchase order
Count the cartons and the items
Look for damage, leaks, wet cartons and expiry dates
Reject or report anything wrong and write it on the delivery note
Sign for what was actually received
Put stock away quickly and update the stock card

blocks.note: Never sign for items you have not counted and checked. If a supplier delivers 18 cartons but the note says 20, write '18 received' and report the shortage.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Storing new stock: first in, first out

blocks.p: Put new stock **behind** the old, so the oldest is used first. This is **FIFO** (first in, first out). It stops items going out of date, and it shows quickly if old stock is not being used.

Supplies are **counted at regular times** (daily in a pantry, weekly or monthly in the store) to check the stock against the records. A supervisor may also do a **spot check** (a count of a few items without warning), which helps to deter theft.

flow: Count the shelf, item by item
Write the count on the count sheet
Compare with the stock card or the record
If there is a difference, recount
Check issue sheets, requisitions and returns
Report any difference that cannot be explained

head: Finding
Likely causes
What to do
rows: Count is lower than the record
Item issued but not written down
Recount, check the paperwork, then report to the supervisor.
Count is higher than the record

blocks.p: Housekeeping chemicals are supplies too. They cost money and can hurt people. You must store, dilute, label and use them correctly.

ul: Keep them in their **original, labelled containers**, closed.
Store them **low down**, so a bottle cannot fall onto someone, and apart from linen, amenities, food and drink.
Keep strong acids and bleach **apart**, so they cannot mix if they leak.
Keep concentrates in a locked store. Do not leave chemicals on a trolley where a guest or child can reach them.
Never pour chemicals into drink or water bottles. Someone may drink them by mistake.

blocks.p: The **label** names the product, shows hazard words and symbols (such as corrosive, irritant, flammable and toxic) and gives instructions. The **safety data sheet (SDS)** gives full information: dangers, PPE, first aid, storage and spills. Read the label every time you use a product. The SDS should be where staff can find it.

Concentrates are mixed with water to the strength on the label. Use a **measuring jug or a dispenser**: this gives the right strength and less waste. Too weak does not clean. Too strong wastes money and can harm skin and surfaces.

Put water in the bottle or bucket first, then add the measured cleaner. Label every spray bottle with the **product name and the dilution**. A bottle with no label is never used: tell your supervisor.

ul: Wear gloves and eye protection when pouring concentrate.
Never mix bleach with ammonia or with acid cleaners such as bowl cleaner: a toxic gas forms.
Use one product at a time.

blocks.note: Splash in the eye: rinse at once with plenty of clean running water for at least 15 minutes and get medical help. Spill on the floor: put a wet floor sign out first, then clean up as the SDS says. Spill on skin: rinse with plenty of water, remove soaked clothing, report it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Dispose of empty chemical containers as the label says. Do not reuse them for another product or for food or drink.

ul: Check plugs and cables on vacuums and irons. A split cord: **stop, tag it 'Do not use' and report it**.
Wash and dry mop heads and cloths after use, so germs and smells do not grow in them. Colour-code cloths so that toilet cloths are never used on cups or glasses.
Heavy cartons (for example a box of 24 bottles) go on a trolley, or you ask for help. Bend your knees, keep your back straight, and hold the load close.
Report items that are damaged or worn out so that they can be repaired or replaced.

blocks.p: Supplies are a big part of housekeeping's cost. Small losses add up fast. Every attendant helps to control them.

ul: Buy and order by the forecast, not by guess.

**Compare unit prices.** A pack of 100 bars at J$6,000 costs J$60 a bar. A pack of 144 bars at J$8,064 costs J$56 a bar, so the second is cheaper per bar, if it will be used before it expires and there is space to store it.
Buying in bulk is cheaper per item, but only if you can store it safely and use it up. Holding far more than needed ties up money and items spoil or go out of date.
Test a **sample** of a new product before ordering a large amount, to check quality and what guests think of it.
Compare supplies used with rooms cleaned (used per occupied room). A sudden rise can show waste or loss early.
Use the amount on the label and the standard list, no more.
Use **refillable dispensers** in showers instead of small bottles, where the property allows.
Do not open items you do not need. Take partly used items back to the store if the rules allow.
Use a towel reuse programme where the property has one: less water, chemicals and energy are used.
Fix leaks and faults early so supplies are not spoiled.
Return unused stock from the trolley at the end of the shift.

blocks.p: **Pilferage** means small, repeated theft of supplies by staff or guests. Prevent it by:

ul: keeping pantries and stores locked and keys controlled (a key log);
recording every issue, with a signature;
counting regularly and checking spot counts against the records;
keeping high-value items (irons, hair dryers, kettles) locked in a cage or cabinet;
not leaving trolleys unattended or doors open;
reporting anyone who takes supplies without permission.

blocks.note: If you see a co-worker taking supplies for personal use, report it to your supervisor. Silence harms honest staff and the property.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Problem
What to do
rows: Expired or nearly expired item (lotion, chemical)
Take it out of use, label it, record it and report it. Do not give it to guests.
Put out a wet floor sign, wear PPE, clean up as the SDS says, record it as damaged and report it.
Stop using it, tag it 'Do not use', report it.
Poor quality delivery (for example toilet rolls that tear)
Keep a sample, set the stock aside, report it to the supervisor.
Set aside, record, report; check the cause (leak, damp).

blocks.note: Record damaged and expired items in the stock records, so the difference between the count and the card is explained.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Working with your team and keeping records

ul: Stock running low before the next delivery: tell your **housekeeping supervisor**.
A guest's special request for extra supplies: supply it and record what you gave.
A fault, damage or loss: report it with the details (item, place, time).
A change in the forecast (an extra group is coming): tell your supervisor, so that stock can be ordered.
Write clearly, with the date, the item, the quantity and your signature.
Correct a mistake with one line through it, the correct entry and your initials.
Keep records in the right place and up to date. Never leave stock records open on a counter.
Return the pantry key and sign the key log at the end of the shift.

blocks.p: A small hotel expects these occupied rooms: Mon 20, Tue 22, Wed 25, Thu 25, Fri 28, Sat 30, Sun 24. Each occupied room gets 2 shampoo bottles a day.
Check the answer: about 25 rooms a day x 7 days = 175, and 175 x 2 = 350. The answer of 348 is sensible.

c1.title: Counting the third-floor pantry in Montego Bay
c1.text: At the end of the day at a Montego Bay hotel, room attendant Kimberly counts the third-floor pantry. The par list says bath soap 90 bars, toilet rolls 120 and hand towels 60. She counts 38 bars of soap, 75 toilet rolls and 60 hand towels. The pantry's stock card shows she should have 41 bars of soap. Heavy bottles of floor cleaner have been left on the top shelf next to the clean hand towels.

c2.title: A busy week at a villa in Port Antonio
c2.text: A 24-room villa property in Port Antonio expects these occupied rooms for next week: Monday 12, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 18, Thursday 18, Friday 20, Saturday 22, Sunday 16. Each occupied room gets 2 toilet rolls and 1 bar of soap a day. The housekeeping store holds 150 toilet rolls and 60 bars of soap. Supervisor Mr. Brown orders once a week and a delivery takes two days.

c3.title: A trolley in a Kingston guest house
c3.text: At a guest house in Kingston, attendant Jermaine finds an unlabelled spray bottle of cloudy liquid on his trolley. A new attendant, Tashana, has poured some concentrated toilet cleaner into an old juice bottle to carry it upstairs, and the juice bottle is on the shelf of the pantry beside the clean towels. The label on the toilet cleaner concentrate says 'Mix 1 part cleaner with 9 parts water'. The spray bottles hold 500 ml.

c4.title: The stock card at a Negril resort
c4.text: At a resort in Negril, the stock card for bottled water cases shows an opening balance of 180 cases on Monday. During the week, 45 cases were issued on Tuesday, 100 cases were received on Wednesday and 30 cases were issued on Friday. On Saturday, supervisor Mrs. Walker does a spot check and counts 190 cases on the shelf. An issue slip from Thursday has a number on it, but no signature.

c5.title: A delivery at a Runaway Bay hotel
c5.text: At a hotel in Runaway Bay, storekeeper Courtney receives a delivery. The delivery note says 20 cartons of bin liners, but he counts 18. One carton of paper towels is wet and stained at the bottom. Behind the shelf, he also finds cartons of old toilet rolls pushed to the back with last year's date. The supplier offers a pack of 100 soap bars at J$6,000 or a pack of 144 bars at J$8,064.

questions.q: How many bars of soap should Kimberly requisition to bring the pantry back to par?
o: 52 bars
38 bars
128 bars
90 bars
questions.why: Requisition = par - stock on hand = 90 - 38 = 52 bars. Writing the quantity with its unit and checking that it makes sense avoids mistakes.

questions.q: How many toilet rolls and hand towels need to be requisitioned?
o: 45 toilet rolls and 60 hand towels
75 toilet rolls and no hand towels
120 toilet rolls and 60 hand towels
45 toilet rolls and no hand towels
questions.why: Toilet rolls: 120 - 75 = 45. Hand towels are already at par (60), so none are needed. Requisition only the shortage.

questions.q: The stock card says 41 bars of soap but Kimberly counts 38. What should she do first?
o: Change the stock card to 38 and say nothing about it
Take 3 bars from the next pantry to even it up
Recount, then check the issue sheets
Accuse the attendant who used the pantry last night
questions.why: A difference may be a counting error or an unrecorded issue. Recount, check the paperwork, and report it if it cannot be explained.

questions.q: What is wrong with how the bottles of floor cleaner have been stored?
o: They should be kept on the top shelf to stay dry
They should be low down and apart from clean linen
They should be on the floor beside the hand towels
They should be unlabelled so guests do not take them
questions.why: Heavy chemical bottles are stored low so they cannot fall, and apart from linen and amenities so a leak cannot spoil or contaminate them.

questions.q: How many toilet rolls will the villa use in the week?
o: 242 toilet rolls
121 toilet rolls
244 toilet rolls
1,694 toilet rolls
questions.why: Room-nights = 12 + 15 + 18 + 18 + 20 + 22 + 16 = 121. Toilet rolls = 121 x 2 = 242. Add up the days first, then multiply.

questions.q: How many extra toilet rolls must Mr. Brown order to cover the week's use?
o: 242 toilet rolls
150 toilet rolls
121 toilet rolls
92 toilet rolls
questions.why: The week needs 242 and the store holds 150, so 242 - 150 = 92 must come in. He should also add a safety amount for the two days a delivery takes.

questions.q: Mr. Brown orders once a week and a delivery takes two days. Why should he keep a safety amount above the forecast?
o: The supplier gives a discount for large orders
Soap and toilet rolls cost more if ordered late
Occupancy can rise or the delivery can be late
Guests use fewer supplies than the forecast shows
questions.why: A forecast is an estimate and deliveries can be late. A safety amount avoids running out, but it should be small, because too much stock ties up money.

questions.q: What is the main danger of the toilet cleaner in the juice bottle?
o: It will lose its smell and look like juice
Someone may drink it by mistake
It will go off if left beside the towels
It will make the bottle weaker over time
questions.why: Chemicals are never put in drink bottles. A bottle of cleaner that looks like juice can be drunk by a guest, child or co-worker.

questions.q: How much concentrate does Jermaine need to fill a 500 ml spray bottle with solution?
o: 50 ml
25 ml
100 ml
450 ml
questions.why: 1 part cleaner + 9 parts water = 10 parts. 500 ml / 10 = 50 ml of cleaner and 450 ml of water.

questions.q: What should Jermaine do with the unlabelled spray bottle on his trolley?
o: Smell it to work out what it is, then use it
Top it up with water and use it as normal
Pour it down the sink straight away
Stop using it and tell his supervisor
questions.why: An unlabelled bottle can be any chemical, and mixing or misusing it can be dangerous. Report it so that it can be identified or disposed of safely.

questions.q: How should the toilet cleaner concentrate be stored?
o: In any clean bottle, as long as it is closed
On the top shelf of the pantry, away from children
Labelled, in its own container, low down in the store
On the trolley, so that it is easy to reach for work
questions.why: Chemicals stay in their original labelled containers, closed, low down and apart from linen and amenities. The juice bottle must never be reused for a chemical.

questions.q: What should the balance on the stock card be on Friday, after all the movements?
o: 175 cases
205 cases
235 cases
325 cases

questions.q: Mrs. Walker counts 190 cases against a card balance of 205. What should she do first?
o: Recount, check the slips, then report any difference
Change the card balance to 190 and carry on working
Order 15 more cases and say nothing to anyone else
Blame the person who counted the stock on Friday
questions.why: A shortage may be a counting error or an unrecorded issue. Recount, check the paperwork, and report any difference that remains.

questions.q: The Thursday issue slip has a quantity but no signature. What is the problem?
o: Nothing: signatures are optional if the number is right
The storekeeper must sign it again at the end of the week
The slip must be thrown away and the stock card changed
There is no proof of who received or approved it
questions.why: A signature shows that the stock was approved and received. Unsigned issues are a common way for small losses to go unnoticed.

questions.q: The note says 20 cartons of bin liners but Courtney counts 18. What should he do?
o: Sign for 20 and hope the supplier makes it up later
Refuse the whole delivery and send it all back to them
Write '18 received' on the note and report the shortage
Sign for 20 and take 2 cartons from the next order
questions.why: Sign only for what you have counted. Writing the shortage on the delivery note gives proof for the supplier and the supervisor.

questions.q: What should Courtney do with the wet, stained carton of paper towels?
o: Dry it in the sun and store it with the rest
Set it aside, record it and report it
Use the towels first, because they are damaged
Put it at the bottom of the stack where it is hidden
questions.why: Damp spoils paper goods and can mean a leak or poor delivery. Set it aside, record it and report it so the supplier or maintenance can act.

questions.q: Which pack gives the lower cost per bar of soap?
o: The 144-bar pack at J$8,064, at J$56 a bar
The 100-bar pack at J$6,000, at J$60 a bar
They cost the same per bar
The 144-bar pack at J$80 a bar
questions.why: J$8,064 / 144 = J$56 and J$6,000 / 100 = J$60. The larger pack is cheaper per bar, but only if it can be stored and used before it spoils.

questions.q: The cartons of old toilet rolls were found pushed to the back. What does this show?
o: The store has too little toilet roll stock
The delivery came in a day early
The old rolls are of better quality
Old stock is not being used first
questions.why: New stock should go behind the old (first in, first out). Old items left at the back are not used and may be spoiled or out of date.

questions.q: A pantry is restocked every 2 days. Daily use of hand soap is 35 bars. What par is needed, with no safety amount?
o: 35 bars
105 bars
70 bars
140 bars
questions.why: Par = daily use x days between restocks = 35 x 2 = 70 bars.

questions.q: Why are consumables such as soap counted differently from durables such as irons?
o: Consumables are always more expensive than durables
Durables are used again, so they can be lost or worn
Durables are used up faster than consumables are
Durables are never counted by the store
questions.why: Consumables are used and finished, so you track how many are left. Durables stay in use, so you track where they are and whether they are lost or worn out.
